analysis.one_liner: Delays for two years the rule requiring retirement advisors to act in savers' best interest.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have put off the Department of Labor's fiduciary rule for two years, never received a House vote and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2016 the Department of Labor issued a rule that broadly defines who counts as a 'fiduciary' for retirement accounts — meaning an advisor who must put your interests ahead of their own. Advisors who earn commissions on the products they recommend would have to meet that standard when advising regular 401(k) and IRA savers, not just pension plans. This bill would have postponed the rule's effective date for two years, keeping the current, weaker standard in place. The bill was referred to two House committees, never received a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill had passed, it would primarily have benefited brokerage firms, commission-based financial advisors, and insurance companies that sell annuities and other commission products into retirement accounts. The delay would have let them keep recommending higher-cost products and collecting commissions without owing customers a best-interest duty, while pushing off the compliance costs of the new rule.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have suspended the effective date of the Department of Labor's April 2016 fiduciary rule for two years from enactment, so advisors to 401(k) and IRA savers would not have had to meet the conflict-of-interest requirements during that period [S2][S3].

The fiduciary rule expands who counts as a fiduciary giving investment advice for compensation, which imposes a legal duty to put plan participants and beneficiaries first in a wider range of advice relationships [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on retirement savers: delaying the rule means two more years of advice that can legally steer people into products carrying higher fees and commissions, which compounds against savings over decades. Regulators and courts also would not have had the clarified standard to enforce.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyday retirement savers paying higher fees

drawbacks.text: Industry groups argued the rule was overly broad and burdensome, and warned it could limit access to affordable advice for lower-balance savers if firms stopped serving small accounts rather than comply — a cost an honest supporter of the rule would acknowledge [S2].
Supporters of the delay argued advisors needed more time to restructure how they are paid and to avoid disruptions for clients mid-transition [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered no benefit to retirement savers; its entire effect was a two-year delay of a rule that requires advisors to serve savers' interests. The best case for it was easing a compliance transition for advisory firms, and the direct cost of that delay in avoidable fees falls on savers themselves. On balance, the bill shifted costs from firms onto the people the rule was written to protect.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Education and the Workforce and Ways and Means committees on introduction day, no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Wilson (R-SC) introduced the bill on January 6, 2017, the first week of the new Congress [S1][S5].
It was referred to the Committee on Education and the Workforce and to the Committee on Ways and Means, with the Speaker to decide which committee would consider it first [S3][S5].
Forty House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].
Neither committee took any further action recorded on the bill — no hearing, markup, or report — and the bill received no floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the two-year delay never took effect through this route, and retirement savers did not lose the best-interest protection through this vehicle. Advisory firms did not get the delay they sought from Congress, though the underlying rule remained contested outside this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Savers who kept the attempted protection

for.name: Rep. Joe Wilson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 6, 2017, to delay the Department of Labor fiduciary rule by two years.

for.name: Financial services and insurance trade groups
for.role: Industry opponents of the fiduciary rule
for.what_they_did: Lobbied against the fiduciary rule and supported legislative efforts to delay or roll it back during the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 41 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on, but the bill never advanced far enough to produce a vote that would show the full partisan split [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have given them two more years without a fiduciary duty to retirement savers, allowing commission-driven product recommendations to continue. Savers pay the difference in fees and returns over time.

industries.industry: Insurance companies selling annuities into IRAs and 401(k)s
industries.note: Annuity sales to retirement savers are heavily commission-based and were among the products most affected by the fiduciary rule. Delaying the rule preserves that sales channel.
